newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left to talk to Renault on doomed car plant.
newsitem.headline: French left to talk to Renault on doomed car plant.

text.p: France's newly elected Socialists plan to hold talks with Renault over the carmaker's controversial decision to shut down a car plant in Belgium, a party spokesman said on Monday.

Renault said in February it would close the Vilvoorde plant to streamline its operations, sparking a storm of protest from Belgian trade unions and politicians and prompting the French Socialists to pledge to try to keep it open if they took power.

"The government will engage in the necessary discussions with Renault," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande told a news conference to discuss the administration's programme after the left's victory in parliamentary elections on Sunday.
"We have said that we do not agree with the decision taken by Renault's chairman and we will see if it is possible to change it in our capacity as a shareholder," Hollande said.
Officials at Renault, 46-percent-controlled by the state, declined to comment.
French newspapers on Saturday quoted Socialists leader Lionel Jospin as saying he would ask Renault to look for ways to keep the plant running.
Belgian trade unions were among the first to congratulate Jospin on the left's election victory and called on the new government to honour its promises.
The left's victory has heartened union representatives, who will hold talks on Tuesday with Renault managers about the plans for the Belgian plant at a European works council meeting.

Renault called the meeting after French and Belgian courts ruled it could not close the plant until it met with the European works council to discuss the shutdown, which Renault says is essential for its economic well-being.
The company reported a 5.25 billion franc loss for 1996, including 3.9 billion in restructuring charges, after a fierce price war in the European car market slashed its margins.

Renault's stock has been weak recently on concerns that a Socialist government could stall or block its restructuring plans, but the share closed up 2.18 percent on Tuesday as part of a broader short-covering rally on the Paris bourse.
